title: A conversation on the mountain
hook: a circle of yogis sits down, and Guru Nanak's long dialogue with them begins

segments.voice: Yesterday the ragas closed, and your line was many moods, one word. Today, a new stretch inside Raga Ramkali.

The circle is already seated when the poem begins. A gathering of Siddhs, yogis who have given up house and family, settle into their postures and greet the company of holy people around them. Then a guest speaks, and his first words aren't to them at all. Guru Nanak bows to the One and says he would cut off his own head and set it down before that One, offering body and mind. Only after that bow does the talking start, and it goes on: question, answer, stanza after stanza.
screen: `THE SIDDHS SIT DOWN.` → `NANAK BOWS TO THE ONE.` → `THEN THE TALKING STARTS.`

segments.voice: The poem is called the Sidh Gosht. Sidh is the yogi, the one said to have reached the goal; gosht is a discussion, a talk. So: the talk with the Siddhs. It sits in the Guru Granth Sahib in Raga Ramkali, under Guru Nanak's name. These yogis have come up on this path before, once in a single picture of a lotus and a duck, once in Bhai Gurdas's telling of their meeting on a mountain, and tradition places the conversation up in those heights. First, this is scripture that keeps the other side's questions. The yogis aren't straw men set up to fall over. They ask real, sharp things, the kind a serious seeker would ask: who are you, why do you live like that, where did it all begin. The Granth sets their questions down in their own voice, some of them by name. Second, the manners. The yogis greet the gathering. Nanak bows before he argues. In the second stanza, in paraphrase, he asks what use there is in wandering about, since it's truth that makes a person pure, and without the Word no one is set free. That's a firm view, said plainly, but said sitting down, in a circle, with people who disagree. Third, the shape teaches. Sikh teaching often comes as song to be sung together. Here it comes as dialogue, two sides taking turns, so listening is built into the form: a question has to be heard all the way through before it can be answered.
screen: `SIDH GOSHT: THE TALK WITH THE SIDDHS.` · `THE YOGIS' QUESTIONS ARE KEPT.` · `NANAK BOWS BEFORE HE ARGUES.` · `DIALOGUE BUILDS IN LISTENING.` · then, large: `A CONVERSATION.`

segments.voice: If you can, play a recording of the first stanzas of the Sidh Gosht; if not, hold the three moves from the hook while the breath slows: the circle sits down, the greeting, the bow. Then bring to mind one conversation waiting for you, and picture the poem's order: sit down with them, greet them, and bow inwardly to what's true. If you pray, let that bow be to the One.
Sidh Gosht. The talk with the Siddhs: Guru Nanak's long dialogue with the yogis in Raga Ramkali, where their questions are kept in their own voice. Today's word.
Your line: a conversation. In this poem, the bow comes before the argument. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: The Sidh Gosht is sung in kirtan and read as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikhs study it in katha, where a teacher explains the yogis' questions and Guru Nanak's answers one stanza at a time.

bow to the One, then take their questions.

what a scholar hears: the Granth keeps a disputation's form, greeting and bow included, so courtesy and disagreement sit in the same text.

chat.says: In the Sidh Gosht, are the yogis just set up so Nanak can knock them down?
options: No. The Granth keeps their sharp questions in their own voice, and Nanak bows before he answers.
Yes. Their questions are left out, and only Nanak's side is recorded in the poem.
No. The yogis do all the teaching, and Nanak just sits quietly and listens.
chat.meaning: The Sidh Gosht keeps the yogis' real questions, some by name. Nanak bows to the One before he argues, and the dialogue builds listening into its form.
